introduction_markdown: Time allowed: two and a half hours. Answer ALL questions. Section I is designed to be answered in 1 hour and Section II in 1 1/2 hours; you are advised to divide your time accordingly. In Section II answer EITHER the a, b and c OR the d, e and f of each question. For your guidance the approximate mark for each part of a question is indicated in brackets. You are reminded of the necessity for good English and orderly presentation in your answers. In calculations you are advised to show all the steps in your working, giving your answer at each stage. Where necessary, assume: the acceleration of free fall, $g = 10\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}$; the speed of light in air, $c = 3\times10^{8}\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$; the charge on an electron, $e = 1.6\times10^{-19}\,\mathrm{C}$. Calculators are allowed.

questions.enonce_markdown:
A glass rod is charged by rubbing with a piece of cloth.

(i) State the type of charge acquired by the glass rod. *[1 mark]*

(ii) Explain the origin of the charge acquired by the rod. *[2 marks]*
questions.corrige_markdown:
**(i)** The glass rod acquires a **positive** charge.

**(ii)** Rubbing makes the two materials touch closely, and **electrons are transferred** from the glass rod to the cloth (the atoms of glass hold their outer electrons less strongly). The rod therefore loses electrons, so it has more protons than electrons and is positively charged. The cloth gains the same number of electrons and becomes negatively charged. Only electrons move; the protons stay fixed in the nuclei.

questions.enonce_markdown:
You are provided with an uncharged metal sphere, A, and a positively charged rod, B, as shown in figure 1.

![fig-1](gce-ol-physics-2025-p2-officiel-cameroun_exercice_2_fig_1.png)

*Figure 1*

(i) Using sketch diagrams outline the steps you would follow to charge the sphere. *[4 marks]*

(ii) Name the method of charging used. *[1 mark]*
questions.corrige_markdown:
**(i)** The sphere is charged by induction in four steps (one sketch for each step):

1. **Bring the rod B near the sphere A without touching it.** The positive rod attracts the free electrons of the metal sphere towards the side nearest to B. Sketch: B on the left, A on its stand; the near side of A marked with minus signs (-), the far side with plus signs (+).
2. **Earth the sphere** while B is still in place, by touching A with a finger (or joining it to the earth with a wire). Electrons flow from the earth to the sphere and neutralise the positive charge on the far side. Sketch: the same picture with a wire or finger from A to the earth symbol; only minus signs remain on A.
3. **Remove the earth connection** (take away the finger or the wire) while B is still near. The sphere is now isolated and keeps its extra electrons.
4. **Take the rod B away.** The extra electrons spread out evenly over the whole surface of the sphere. Sketch: A with minus signs all around its surface.

The sphere A ends up with an excess of electrons, so it carries a **negative** charge (the sign opposite to that of the charging rod).

**(ii)** The method is **charging by (electrostatic) induction**.
